instructions: 'Prompt version: article-claims-v2.


  You extract atomic claims from one article so a person can fact-check them later.
  You do not search, and you do not assign a verdict.


  Return only JSON:

  {"claims":[{"id":"c1","source_quote":"exact substring of the article","normalized_claim":"one
  standalone claim","category":"checkable_fact|opinion|prediction|needs_context","missing_context":[],"verification_scope":"external_fact|document_content|text_analysis"}]}


  Rules:

  - source_quote must be copied character for character from the article. Do not fix
  spelling, and do not join text from two places.

  - Split a sentence that states two independent facts into two claims. Each quote
  must still be an exact substring.

  - Keep limiters in normalized_claim: some, all, only, may, as of a date, a named
  exam, a team, a tier, or a price category.

  - Preserve the source quote''s asserted meaning in normalized_claim: keep its subject,
  action, polarity, tense, certainty, time, quantities, and scope. Do not weaken a
  forecast into a present fact, strengthen a possibility into certainty, reverse a
  negation, or omit a limiting phrase. If a faithful normalization is unclear, use
  the source wording and explain the missing context.

  - Extract statements about the limits of current knowledge as claims too. Phrases
  such as "unknown," "unclear," "not known," or "no data" assert a state of knowledge;
  do not omit them or turn them into a claim that an event or object did not exist.
  Preserve whose knowledge is limited, which aspect is unknown, and any stated time
  or scope.

  - Do not add ordinal or superlative limits such as “first,” “earliest,” or “only”
  unless the quote or one clear context explicitly states them. Never turn an unordered
  event into a first event.

  - In normalized_claim, resolve a pronoun or demonstrative such as "it", "they",
  "these actions", "that exam", "the same report", "the paper", or "that date" from
  the article context only when there is one clear antecedent. Preserve the source
  quote exactly. If the antecedent is ambiguous or absent, keep the claim cautious
  and list the missing referent in missing_context; never guess.

  - Do not replace a claim with a neighboring sentence while resolving context. The
  normalized claim must preserve the source quote''s subject, predicate, numbers,
  and direction. If the quote is "These actions allowed X to flourish", do not turn
  it into a claim about how a release was licensed. Keep the causal assertion and
  list any unclear action, concrete outcome or measure, and causal basis in missing_context.

  - For causal language such as "caused", "allowed", "enabled", "led to", or "resulted
  in", check whether the article names the action, outcome, and a concrete indicator.
  Vague outcomes such as "flourish" or "improve" need the missing object or measure
  and evidence for the causal link listed in missing_context. Do not treat temporal
  order alone as causal proof.

  - When a claim reports that headlines or another speaker described a gain, improvement,
  score, or other result with a comparison, preserve that attribution and identify
  the result or measure being described. If the article does not make the referent
  clear, include it in missing_context instead of guessing.

  - If the article attributes the statement, keep that attribution in source_quote
  and in normalized_claim. Phrases to keep include "the report says", "the authors
  add", "according to", "I think", and "headlines called". Do not turn an attributed
  statement into a bare fact.

  - Keep a statement''s existing speaker, source, role, and attribution verb when
  the article supplies them. If the attribution is outside quotation marks or is carried
  by a clearly connected continuation, make source_quote one exact contiguous substring
  that includes the statement and enough attribution context; keep the same attribution
  in normalized_claim. Do not infer a speaker or source when the article leaves it
  unclear.

  - Do not extend an attribution across "and". "The report says A, and B" supports
  "The report says A". It does not support "The report says B". Leave B as its own
  claim without that attribution.

  - Preserve semantic relationships between the subject, action, object, and any necessary
  participants. Keep stated spatial and directional relationships (for example, which
  place or object is inside, beside, connected to, or leads to another), as well as
  causal direction. When splitting independent facts, make each claim''s quote and
  normalization retain the relationship needed to understand that fact; do not keep
  only a measurement or outcome while dropping the action or connection that gives
  it meaning.

  - Preserve appositive definitions and relationships that identify a place or entity,
  likelihood qualifiers such as "rarer", "alternatively", and "usually", and qualifications
  about a speaker''s role or independence. A quote must begin at a sentence or clause
  boundary that retains these qualifiers. For a continued quotation, carry the speaker
  only when the article makes the continuation explicit in the same paragraph; otherwise
  list the missing speaker in missing_context without guessing.

  - Include checkable method, data, and sample facts, including data spans, sample
  sizes, and model inputs when stated. Keep each as a source-grounded claim; do not
  add details the article does not state.

  - A price claim needs the named product or service being billed. Fill that name
  only when the price clause in the article states it. If it does not, list the missing
  product or service in missing_context. Do not borrow a name from the other half
  of an "and" sentence.

  used a phrase needs the headline, not proof that the phrase''s comparison is true.

  document says, lists, does not say, or does not report. It is text_analysis when
  the sentence classifies another line as a forecast, preference, or opinion. Otherwise
  it is external_fact.

{"article": "Two ‘forever chemicals’ associated with higher risk of aggressive breast cancer in NIH analysis
Thursday, November 5, 2026
Evidence continues to grow on how environmental factors affect women’s health.
Women with higher blood levels of two common per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, also familiarly known as PFAS, were more likely to develop estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer, according to a new study by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). PFAS are a large group of chemicals used in common consumer products. Often referred to as “forever chemicals,” PFAS do not break down easily in the environment and can remain in the body for years.
The study found that women with higher blood plasma levels of two of these substances, perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), were associated with a higher incidence of ER-negative breast cancer. No clear association was observed between the two chemicals and breast cancer risk overall.
“Women deserve clear answers about how chemicals in their environment may affect their health,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “This NIH study links two forever chemicals to a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer and demands further investigation. Under President Trump’s leadership, we will pursue the evidence, confront environmental health risks, and give women the information they need to protect their health.”
ER-negative tumors lack receptors that allow hormone estrogen to help cancer cells grow. Compared with breast cancers that respond to hormone estrogen, ER-negative breast cancers tend to be more aggressive and have worse outcomes. Scientists know less about what raises the risk of this type of breast cancer.
“Our findings, which we confirmed using a meta-analysis of prior research, indicate that certain legacy PFAS, including PFOA and PFOS, are associated with a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer, a more aggressive tumor type with few known risk factors,” explained NIH Stadtman Investigator Alexandra White, Ph.D., who led the study. The findings are reported in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.
NIH researchers and their collaborators measured 17 PFAS in blood, collected years before women were diagnosed with cancer. Women in the group with the highest PFOA levels had a 67% higher rate of ER-negative breast cancer than those in the lowest group. For PFOS, the rate was 93% higher, or nearly twice as high. These numbers describe relative differences between groups, not an individual woman’s chance of getting breast cancer.
The research drew on the Sister Study, led by NIH’s National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS). The larger study enrolled 50,884 women ages 35–74 in the United States and Puerto Rico from 2003 to 2009. None had breast cancer when they joined the Sister Study, but each had a full or half-sister who had been previously diagnosed with breast cancer. For the PFAS study, researchers included 1,609 women who developed breast cancer and a comparison sample of 2,269 women.
“These findings matter for women’s health broadly,” said first author, Che-Jung Chang, Ph.D., a former research fellow at NIH and a current researcher at DLH, a scientific research organization. “Although PFAS are persistent in the environment and in our bodies, exposure to them is still potentially modifiable, meaning people can take steps to reduce their exposure, and these findings could open new avenues for prevention.”
Because the strongest associations involved tumors without hormone receptors, the authors suggest that PFAS may affect cancer risk through other non-hormonal biologic pathways. Possible pathways include changes in gene activity or immune system. However, this study did not test those explanations. The authors say future studies should evaluate people with higher PFAS exposure and in groups more affected by ER-negative breast cancer.
Although most individuals have measurable levels of PFOA and PFOS in their bodies, these compounds have been largely phased out and replaced with new PFAS compounds. “More research is needed, particularly evaluating the risk of breast cancer associated with newer replacement PFAS chemicals,” White said.
This research was supported by NIEHS grants: Z01ES044005; Z1AES103332; and R01ES032831.", "repair_errors": []}

{"article": "First-time homebuyers remain scarce, but a record share of them pay all cash
November 5, 2026 10:00 AM ET Heard on Morning Edition Jennifer Ludden
The share of first-time homebuyers remains at a near-record low of 22% as a housing shortage and high prices sideline many, according to a new report by the National Association of Realtors. But those who are managing to buy are older and wealthier than in the past, and 1 in 10 paid all cash, a record high since such data was collected starting in 2003.
"Inheritances are really driving this," said Jessica Lautz, deputy chief economist at the NAR.
First-time buyers who paid all-cash were more likely than those who financed a house to use an inheritance (28%) or proceeds from the sale of an inherited property (21%). They were also older.
NAR finds the median age of all first-time buyers remains at 40, a record high. For first-time buyers who financed a purchase it was 38, while for those who paid all-cash it was 54. "They waited a significant period of time for that generational transfer of wealth to come through," Lautz said.
For first-time buyers overall, personal savings was the biggest source of funding for a down payment. But in another shift, more people used assets – like a 401(k), stocks, or cryptocurrency – than financial help from family or friends. Older buyers have had more time to save up, Lautz said, but she thinks there's another factor: "I think it's uncomfortable to ask mom and dad for a gift or loan when you're hitting 40 versus your young 30s."
The share of first time buyers using an inheritance is likely to grow in coming years as boomers reach their 80's and beyond. As the report noted, "there is a growing divide among those who are saving independently and priced out of homeownership, versus those who are waiting on the sidelines but then given a generational transfer of wealth."
Real estate agents around the country are seeing the change.
"I would say in the first 15 years of my career, I saw virtually zero first-time home buyers paying all cash," said Jason Miller, a broker with Trust Real Estate Company in St. Cloud, Minn.
But he's had a number of them since the COVID-19 pandemic, when homebuying surged. "They knew they had to absolutely have the most sterling offer possible to compete in the competitive marketplace," he said.
High mortgage rates are also driving all-cash bids, Miller said, since they make it far more expensive to finance a home for 30 years. And not all families wait until death to pass on wealth.   action, polarity, tense, certainty, time, quantities, and scope. Do not weaken a
  forecast into a present fact, strengthen a possibility into certainty, reverse a

  the source wording and explain the missing context.

  do not omit them or turn them into a claim that an event or object did not exist.
  Preserve whose knowledge is limited, which aspect is unknown, and any stated time
  or scope.

  - Do not add ordinal or superlative limits such as “first,” “earliest,” or “only”

  event into a first event.

  normalized claim must preserve the source quote''s subject, predicate, numbers,
  and direction. If the quote is "These actions allowed X to flourish", do not turn
  it into a claim about how a release was licensed. Keep the causal assertion and
  list any unclear action, concrete outcome or measure, and causal basis in missing_context.

  and evidence for the causal link listed in missing_context. Do not treat temporal
  order alone as causal proof.
